newsitem.title: INDIA: India says top foreign policy priority is economy.
newsitem.headline: India says top foreign policy priority is economy.

text.p: India's top foreign policy priority is to strengthen its economy, and New Delhi is prepared to buy arms from any suitable supplier, Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral said on Thursday.
"Indian foreign policy gives the highest priority to the economy, economic growth and economic relations," Gujral told Asian News International in an interview released to Reuters.
He said that in the post-Cold War world, every country assigned the highest priority to its economy and "therefore foreign policy must protect that".

The foreign minister said India, which during the Cold War depended on the Soviet Union for outside weapons supplies, buys arms "wherever we find them suitable ... price-wise and technology-wise, wherever we can buy".

"Today's world market of arms is open and we do not have any tilts in that," he said. "Therefore we have an open-door policy, wherever we think it suits us and whatever quality and technology suits us, we go for that."
Gujral, who began his second stint as foreign minister when Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda took office last June, said the government had emphasised regional cooperation.
"Our relations with Bangladesh have undergone dramatic change," he said, adding that India had strengthened ties with Central Asia, South Asia and Southeast Asia.
"Similarly our relations with Russia are very good. We are improving our relations with America even further."
Gujral defended New Delhi's decision to oppose the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT) which bans nuclear test explosions, saying India was surrounded by nuclear powers.
"China is a nuclear state. Diego Garcia is a nuclear weapons base," he said, referring to the U.S. base in the Indian Ocean.

He added that the Middle East Gulf was awash with arms "and Pakistan is known to be acquiring something with the help of China. In these circumstances, it is not possible for India to surrender its options".

Asked to comment on India's recent failure to win a seat on the United Nations Security Council, Gujral cited Delhi's lone opposition to the CTBT and said: "This is the price every country pays for standing up on its own dignity and preserving its national interest."
